title: A passing check that couldn't fail
dek: Xeno shows whether an AI agent's passing check was actually tested, on its row in Herdr and on the claim's line in your editor.

evidence.note: The plugin's tests start a Herdr server and read each pane's lights back. They run in CI but don't yet block a merge.
The agents' diffs and Jev's scores are recordings, replayed through the real plugin.

evidence.what: A live run, agents and Jev included
evidence.note: When it runs, it will be published on this site as a check, with its prediction registered first.

blocks: An agent reported that people can install witness, my language server for verification findings. Its check passed.
This is what the check ran:

blocks.text:
$ cd /tmp/feature && bash install.sh
Installing Go 1.24 for witness...
witness installed to /usr/local/bin/witness

blocks: That isn't how people install witness. They add its dev container feature, which gets Go from another feature it depends on. The check ran the install script in a container that already had Go, so it would have passed whether or not that dependency worked.
The check was accurate about what it saw. It was never in a position to fail.

sections.heading: Verifiers and falsifiers
blocks: A passing check is a verifier: it looks for evidence that the claim is true. On its own, it can't show that it would have noticed the claim being false.

That takes a falsifier: a run that tries to make the claim false. Here, that means removing the dependency and installing the feature again. If the install still succeeds, the check could never have failed. If it breaks, the check can fail, and its pass now carries information.

Both runs still aren't enough when an agent performs them, because an agent can report a falsifier that didn't really try. So a third reader, Jev, a scoring model from TypeSafe, is given both runs' diffs and asked how likely it is that both were genuine.

sections.heading: Three lights
blocks: Xeno is a plugin for Herdr, a terminal multiplexer for agents. An agent reports each run from its own pane:

blocks.text:
xeno verifier confirmed   # or failed
xeno falsifier failed     # or refuted
xeno jev 0.9              # Jev: were both runs genuine?

blocks: Each agent's row in the Herdr sidebar shows three lights, in the order of a macOS window's buttons: red for the falsifier, amber for Jev, green for the verifier. A lit light means that run has reported. The colours don't mean pass or fail.
Beside the lights is a status. The first two need attention:

blocks.text:
uncontrolled  a run hasn't reported
unverified    both reported; Jev missing or below 0.7
confirmed     on target; verifier confirmed, falsifier failed
refuted       on target; the falsifier won
inconclusive  on target; neither run got its way

blocks: A refuted run is still on target: the prediction was wrong, but it was properly tested.

sections.heading: The witness check, three ways
blocks: Tell xeno where the claim is and it also writes a witness finding on that line, so the status appears in your editor, with each run's diff a go-to-definition away.

blocks.text:
$ xeno claim check.go:9
$ xeno verifier confirmed today.diff
uncontrolled

blocks: First, the original passing check on its own. Only the verifier has reported, so the run is uncontrolled, shown as a warning on the claim's line.

blocks.text:
$ xeno falsifier failed falsifier.diff
$ xeno jev 0.3
unverified

blocks: Next, the falsifier removes the dependency, and the install breaks. Both runs have now reported, but Jev, comparing them, doubts that the verifier installed witness the way people do. The run is unverified, and the warning becomes an error.

blocks.text:
$ xeno verifier confirmed verifier.diff
$ xeno jev 0.9
confirmed

blocks: Finally, a verifier that installs it properly: it starts a dev container with the witness feature and finds the binary. Jev scores both runs as genuine, the run is confirmed, and the finding drops to information level.
The check passed in all three runs. Xeno reported uncontrolled, unverified and confirmed.

sections.heading: Limits
blocks: The example is a replay. The diffs are recordings of agent runs, and Jev's scores are recorded too. The plugin itself is real: it runs in Herdr, lights the panes and writes the findings, and its tests check this against a running Herdr server.

So this article shows how xeno reads a run. It doesn't show that a live agent and a live Jev get this case right. That is the next check. It will be published here with its prediction registered before it runs, whatever the result.
The source is in null-hype/features, under src/xeno.
